title: Peddi Made ₹150 Crore in Two Days. Then India Noticed What It Did to Janhvi Kapoor.
excerpt: Director Buchi Babu Sana has apologized and promised to re-edit scenes after viewers called out the hypersexualization of Janhvi's character. The film is a hit. The conversation is bigger.
body:
The camera lingers on Janhvi Kapoor's body like it's the only thing worth looking at. In scene after scene of Peddi, director Buchi Babu Sana's rural sports drama that has otherwise announced itself as one of 2026's biggest box office events, the framing reduces its female lead to decoration — a beautiful woman filmed as though the audience paid specifically to stare at her.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=noatJVfA22U

Two days in, the film had crossed ₹150 crore worldwide. Ram Charan had delivered the performance of his career — physical, ferocious, the kind of leading-man work that justifies a ₹200 crore budget. The reviews were glowing. The numbers were staggering. And then the conversation shifted.

https://x.com/BuchiBabuSana/status/2063105976535015933

The Scene That Broke It

Viewers zeroed in on a sequence where Ram Charan's character kisses Janhvi's character without consent, leaving her visibly distressed. In isolation, it might have registered as a dramatic beat. But it wasn't in isolation. It sat alongside repeated close-ups of Kapoor's body, camera angles that prioritized skin over story, and a romantic track that several critics argued normalized harassment as courtship.

"One of the biggest issues of the Janhvi scenes in Peddi beyond the fact that it's absolutely hopeless and disgusting is the fact that psychologically you aren't able to even lock back into the movie after her scenes are done because you are so disgusted." — @Ganeshen5 on X

The backlash was swift, loud, and came from everywhere — film critics, social media commentators, and audiences who had walked into theatres expecting a sports drama and walked out uncomfortable.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZMi_VhCGaF/

The Director Responds

On June 6, Buchi Babu Sana posted a statement on X that landed somewhere between apology and damage control. "As a filmmaker, I believe cinema should entertain, inspire, and connect with audiences," he wrote. "It should never make anyone feel uncomfortable or disrespected."

He confirmed that changes would be made to "the concerned portions" — a rare mid-run admission from a director whose film is actively minting money. The revised cut will replace the current version in theatres, though no timeline was specified.

"Every woman deserves to be respected, valued, and represented with dignity. We remain committed to telling stories that celebrate strong characters and uphold those values." — Buchi Babu Sana

It is, by any measure, an extraordinary thing for a filmmaker to do while his movie is still in its opening week. The film is not struggling. It is not being pulled from screens. It is printing money. And yet here is its director, publicly acknowledging that parts of it are indefensible.

The Bigger Pattern

Peddi is not the first Indian film to treat its heroine as set dressing. It is not even the first Ram Charan film to draw this criticism. But what makes this moment different is the speed and intensity of the pushback — and the fact that the industry actually responded.

For decades, mainstream Indian cinema has operated on a formula where the hero transforms, trains, fights, and earns his arc, while the heroine exists to be beautiful in the background. The "item number" became its own genre. Close-ups of women's bodies were not subtext — they were the text.

What has changed is the audience. A generation that grew up on the same films now watches them through a lens shaped by global conversations about consent, representation, and the male gaze. They are not asking for sanitized cinema. They are asking for cinema where women are people.

What This Means for Diaspora Audiences

For NRI viewers who watch Telugu and Hindi cinema as a connection to home, these conversations hit differently. Many grew up with these tropes — the rain song, the chase sequence played for romance, the heroine whose primary job was to look stunning in six outfits. Seeing them called out in real time is both vindicating and complicated.

Peddi is available in Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, Kannada, and Malayalam across theatres in North America, the UK, and Australia. It will almost certainly cross ₹250 crore worldwide. The question is whether the version that gets there will be the one playing now or the one Buchi Babu promised.

The film is a hit. Janhvi Kapoor deserved better from it. Both things are true at the same time.
